rashi:a1.1: This is what it is saying: One consecrates limbs and one substitutes for them, etc.: That is, one consecrates one limb, and afterward one substitutes [another animal] for that animal. And this “and one substitutes for them” teaches us that when it says “one consecrates limbs,” it does not mean one who consecrates a limb by itself, but that the sanctity spreads through the whole animal. For if it referred to the limb alone, it could not say “and one substitutes for them,” since even Rabbi Yosei, who says one substitutes limbs for whole peace offerings, concedes that one does not substitute whole animals for them, and all the more so limbs for limbs. And what the latter clause of this teaching in the second chapter [16b–17a] teaches, “but one does not substitute,” teaches us that one does not substitute [limbs] for whole animals: if he said, “The limb of this animal is a substitute,” he has not consecrated it. And this is the stringency of initial consecration over substitution: in initial consecration, when he consecrates one limb, [the sanctity] spreads through all of it; but in substitution, when he says, “This limb is a substitute in place of this whole animal,” it is not consecrated.
rashi:a1.2: And fetuses that were consecrated in their mother’s womb: For example, offspring of sacrificial animals. Even though they are consecrated, one does not substitute an animal for them as long as they are in their mother’s womb. And this is not taught as a stringency of sacrificial animals over substitution; rather, since the tanna taught “and one substitutes for them” with regard to an animal consecrated through a limb, he taught with regard to fetuses that one does not substitute for them. And it is Rabbi Yehuda, [who says that] the offspring effects substitution; for if it were the Rabbis, [the offspring] does not effect substitution even outside [the womb].
tosafot:a1.1: This is what it is saying: One consecrates limbs and one substitutes: This is Rashi’s reading, and it means: if the sanctity spread through the whole animal by means of the sanctity of [the limb], one substitutes for the whole animal; but if he said, “This limb of a non-sacred animal shall be a substitute,” he has said nothing. And it seems that this is why Rashi was pressed to read “and one substitutes”: because shortly after, [the Gemara] asks on it, “Are limbs consecrated?” For if he did not read “and one substitutes,” where do we find that it says limbs are consecrated? Rather, from the fact that it says one substitutes [for] limbs, it is necessarily where he consecrated the limb and the sanctity spread through the whole animal. But it does not seem correct to read “and one substitutes”: first, because it is not in most books; and furthermore, because in the mishna it is taught among the things more stringent in initial consecration than in substitution, and if one reads “and one substitutes,” this is not a stringency of initial consecration over substitution. Therefore it seems that one does not read it. And as for what [the Gemara] asks on it shortly after, “Are limbs consecrated?”, that is because it teaches “one consecrates fetuses and limbs,” and certainly he could not consecrate a limb alone unless the sanctity spread through the whole animal.
gershom:a1.1: It teaches thus: One consecrates limbs and one substitutes for them.
gershom:a2.1: And fetuses that were consecrated in their mother’s womb: For example, where he consecrated them [i.e., the mothers] and afterward they became pregnant; one does not substitute for them. And in fact this too deals with offspring of sacrificial animals, [but with regard to ordinary fetuses one cannot yet infer from it that they are consecrated].
gershom:a3.1: If it is Rabbi Yehuda: Say the first clause: “One consecrates limbs and one substitutes for them.” But how can one substitute for them? Rabbi Yehuda does not hold that one who says, “The leg of this animal is a burnt offering,” makes all of it a burnt offering, and so too with regard to substitution.
gershom:a4.1: He said to him: Rabbi Zeira [said]: But Rabbi Yehuda concedes that if he consecrated a limb upon which life depends, all of it is consecrated, and it is with regard to that limb that it says “one consecrates limbs and one substitutes for them.” And in fact it deals with offspring of sacrificial animals.
gershom:a5.1: Another version: “But one does not substitute”: In any event it teaches “one consecrates fetuses.” He said to him: For example, where he consecrated them for their value, and likewise [with regard to limbs, where he consecrated the limbs for their value]. And the reason one does not substitute is that he consecrated them for their value; but had he consecrated them inherently, they would be consecrated so as to effect substitution. But Rabbi Yehuda said that limbs are not consecrated so that the whole animal becomes a substitute, so one cannot establish [the mishna] in accordance with Rabbi Yehuda. He said to him: When we learned “one consecrates [fetuses,” it is teaching about offspring of sacrificial animals. “If offspring of sacrificial animals,” etc.], as we answered above in the first version.
tosafot:a5.1: One who slaughters the sin offering: For example, a female goat; for a ewe cannot give birth within its first year, as stated in Bekhorot (19b).
tosafot:a5.2: And he found in it a live four-month-old: For a five-month-old [fetus] in a small animal is not permitted by the slaughter of its mother according to the Rabbis, [as stated in] the chapter Behema HaMaksha (Ḥullin 74a).
gershom:a6.1: [And he found in it] a live four-month-old: It is dealing with a small animal, which is pregnant for five months.
rashi:a5.1: Only by the males of the priesthood: As is the law of a sin offering. It enters our mind [at this stage] that we are dealing with one who designates a pregnant animal. For if it were one who designates an empty animal and it became pregnant, everyone would agree that since [the fetus] is consecrated by the power of its mother, it is non-sacred, as offspring of sacrificial animals are sanctified at their coming into being, when they are born, and not in their mother’s womb.
rashi:a6.1: What, is it not a dispute of tanna’im: For according to the first tanna, sanctity takes effect on the limbs [i.e., on the fetus] by their own power: when it was pregnant at the time of consecration, [the fetus] is consecrated immediately, and it is not like the [ordinary] offspring of sacrificial animals. And according to the latter tanna, sanctity takes effect on it only through the power of its mother, and it is like other offspring of sacrificial animals, which are sanctified at their coming into being. And that is why it specified “alive”: it is a novelty. It teaches us that we do not say: since it is alive, this counts as its coming into being, so that even according to the latter tanna it should be consecrated through the power of its mother like other offspring of sacrificial animals. It teaches us that since its months were not complete, this is not its coming into being.
rashi:a7.1: No: [The baraitot] are not dealing at all with one who designates a pregnant animal, but with a sacrificial animal that became pregnant. And this is what they disagree about: the first tanna holds that offspring of sacrificial animals are sanctified at their coming into being, when they are born, and not in their mother’s womb. [Rashi’s “first tanna” is the first view stated in the Gemara’s answer; the Davidson English assigns this view to the second baraita.]
rashi:a7.2: At their coming into being [bahavayatan]: It uses the language of the verse from which offspring are included, as it is written: “Only your sacred things which you have [asher yihyu lekha]” (Deuteronomy 12:26), and the Master said: “Which you have”: these are the offspring, in the second chapter of Bekhorot (14b).
gershom:a7.1: At their coming into being they are sacred: At the time they emerge into the air of the world. And in the latter [baraita], where he consecrated [the animal] and in the end it became pregnant, the offspring is not consecrated, since only the mother alone was consecrated, etc. [The printed text, which an editor’s note corrects to the reading above, has instead: where it became pregnant and in the end he consecrated it, the offspring is not consecrated, since he consecrated only the mother alone.]
rashi:a8.1: And if you wish, say it is one tanna: [Who taught] these two baraitot, and everyone agrees that sanctity takes effect on fetuses immediately, in accordance with Rabbi Yoḥanan. And the one that teaches that the fetus is not consecrated is where one consecrates an animal and afterward it became pregnant, since offspring of sacrificial animals are sanctified at their coming into being. And the one that teaches that the offspring is consecrated immediately, and is not like other offspring of sacrificial animals, [is where] he consecrated [the mother] when pregnant, since a fetus is not the thigh of its mother.
rashi:a9.1: They are not sacred as a substitute: That if they are non-sacred and he exchanged them for a sacrificial animal, they are not seized [by sanctity]. And even substitution, which takes effect on animals with permanent blemishes, does not take effect on them; and all the more so if he actually consecrated them, they are not consecrated.
rashi:a9.2: And they do not sanctify: Another animal to make it a substitute, if they are consecrated and he exchanged a non-sacred animal for them. And Rabbi Meir explains how it can be found that they are consecrated: since they are not consecrated with any inherent sanctity, from where would they sanctify and effect substitution? They are mere wood!
gershom:a8.1: [They are not sacred to become a substitute for sacrificial animals, and they do not sanctify to effect substitution: for if the sacrificial animals are diverse kinds or a tereifa, they are not strong enough to be consecrated so as to seize a non-sacred animal as their substitute.]
gershom:a9.1: It is taught: “Rabbi … said”: This refers back to [the statement of] Rabbi Elazar. [Rabbeinu Gershom’s heading gives only “Rabbi,” where the daf has Rabbi Meir, and his text names Rabbi Elazar where the daf has Rabbi Eliezer.]
rashi:a10.1: You find only: [A case] where they are sacred, so that it was necessary to teach “they do not sanctify,” where one consecrates an animal and afterward it became a tereifa. And this is a sanctity that preceded its blemish.
gershom:a10.1: [Rather,] you find: That it was necessary to say “and they do not sanctify” only where one consecrates an animal and afterward it became a tereifa, [for initially it was consecrated when it was whole, and now that it has become a tereifa it does not sanctify to effect substitution].
rashi:a10.2: Where one consecrates an offspring: In its mother’s womb, so that sanctity takes effect on it immediately, and afterward it emerged by caesarean section.
gershom:a11.1: And likewise where one consecrates an offspring: In its mother’s womb, and afterward it emerged by caesarean section, [it does not sanctify so as to seize a substitute]. But a tereifa [from the outset], before consecration, and one born by caesarean section, after it was born, are not consecrated as sacrificial animals. And this one emerged by caesarean section after he consecrated it. [And this “and afterward it emerged by caesarean section” is, for example, where the walls of the womb were cut or torn away. Evidently the offspring is consecrated in its mother’s womb, and this is a refutation of bar Padda.]
rashi:a11.1: These needed to be stated: That they do not sanctify. And the conclusion of the matter is explained in the chapter Yesh BaKorbanot (below, Temurah 17a).
gershom:a12.1: They say: With an unblemished fetus in the womb of an unblemished mother, even bar Padda concedes to Rabbi Yoḥanan that it is consecrated, similar to this case of one who consecrates an offspring and afterward it emerged by caesarean section], which is an unblemished one in the womb of an unblemished mother, as long as it is in her womb. They disagreed only, etc.
rashi:a12.1: Diverse kinds, a tumtum and a hermaphrodite, you find only with offspring of sacrificial animals: That a sacrificial animal became pregnant with them after its consecration. Evidently a fetus is consecrated, since it teaches [the case of] one who consecrates a fetus and it emerges by caesarean section: it is this one that is not consecrated inherently so as to effect substitution, but if it did not emerge by caesarean section, it is consecrated with the first sanctity, inherent sanctity, and effects substitution. And one cannot answer [that it refers to] sanctity of value, for if it were sanctity of value it would not effect substitution even if it emerged by way of the womb.
gershom:a13.1: Another version: But a tumtum [and diverse kinds and a hermaphrodite, you find only, etc.]: That is, these two, a tereifa and one born by caesarean section, you can establish even [where they were] non-sacred, as we said. But diverse kinds, a tumtum and a hermaphrodite you do not find among sacrificial animals that are consecrated, except with offspring of sacrificial animals, with fetuses of sacrificial animals, for these never had a time of fitness: from the time of their formation they were disqualified [they were formed as diverse kinds, tumtum or hermaphrodite], and they were consecrated only by virtue of their mothers. That is why it says “you find only with offspring of sacrificial animals,” and it is in accordance with Rabbi Yehuda, who says the offspring effects substitution.
gershom:a14.1: It is these that are not consecrated inherently: But only by virtue of their mothers, for they are consecrated only for their value, since they are blemished. But other fetuses [the text repeats itself here] are consecrated inherently, even in the womb of their non-sacred mothers. And this is difficult for bar Padda. Abaye said: With an unblemished one in the womb of an unblemished mother, etc., as above.
rashi:b2.1: Shall be sacred: That limb. And since that limb is sacred, he can no longer slaughter that animal as non-sacred; rather, all of it shall be sold except for the value of that limb in it. For he does not take the value of that limb, since he consecrated it and cannot sell it.
rashi:b2.2: This is how we read: The statement of Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda.
gershom:b1.1: [But he is bringing] an animal lacking a limb: Since initially a limb of it was consecrated.
rashi:b4.1: Lacking a limb: For that limb is not his; rather, it is sacrificed for the obligation of the seller. It emerges that this purchaser did not sacrifice a whole burnt offering, though he vowed to sacrifice the whole animal for his obligation.
rashi:b4.2: Where he says: It is incumbent upon me to bring a burnt offering with its life: It is incumbent upon me to sacrifice all the limbs from which the animal lives. And he has done so, for the seller consecrated only a limb from which it does not live, for example, the leg from the knee joint downward. For had he consecrated a thing upon which life depends, the sanctity would have spread through all of it, as it says: Rabbi Yehuda concedes with regard to a thing that renders it a tereifa, that if he consecrated a limb whose removal would render it a tereifa, the sanctity spreads through all of it even according to Rabbi Yehuda. Another version, [from the] Jerusalem [Talmud]: “But he is bringing an animal whose body he consecrates when it is not all his”; that is, this purchaser is bringing an animal whose body is not [entirely] his. And it answers: For example, where he said, “A zuz’s worth of this animal for a burnt offering,” that is, a zuz’s worth of this animal as a burnt offering, and he has acquired a zuz’s worth. Therefore he has fulfilled [his vow], for he did not vow a whole burnt offering.
gershom:b2.1: [Ravina said: Where he says: This purchaser says at the time of his vow: It is incumbent upon me to bring a burnt offering.] [Rabbeinu Gershom’s text reads Ravina here, where the daf has Rava.]
gershom:b3.1: With its life: That is, (where this purchaser says at the time of his vow:) It is incumbent upon me (an animal) to bring a burnt offering that can live; and even though it was lacking that [limb] that was consecrated earlier, it could live, and he has brought what he vowed. Another version: “But he is bringing an animal,” etc. [Rather, Rava said: For example, where he said at the time of his vow: It is incumbent upon me] a zuz’s worth (that is, at the time of his vow he said only a zuz’s worth) of [this] animal as a burnt offering, [for he took upon himself only a zuz’s worth of it as a burnt offering]. Now, [apart] from that consecrated limb, [it is still] worth several zuz, and he can bring [what is worth more]. [The note ends with the words “Rabbi Yehuda concedes,” which head the next passage.]
rashi:b5.1: Rabbi Yehuda concedes: That the sanctity spreads through all of it.
gershom:b4.1: With regard to a thing upon which life depends: [For if he consecrated a limb of it upon which life depends,] for example, the heart or the liver, [all of it is consecrated; or] with regard to a thing that renders it a tereifa [if that limb is removed from it, for example,] where its leg was cut off from the knee joint upward.
rashi:b5.2: That renders it a carcass: For example, the thigh and its recess. But with regard to a thing that renders it a tereifa, such as its leg from the knee joint upward, he does not concede, and the reason is explained below. [A further gloss follows, apparently on Rav Sheshet’s “that it dies”:] For example, the heart or the gullet.
gershom:b5.1: And Rava holds: In accordance with the one who says a tereifa can survive. That is why he says “with regard to a thing that renders it a carcass,” for example, where the thigh and its recess were removed, [which is a carcass].
rashi:b6.1: In accordance with the one who says a tereifa cannot survive: It is a dispute in the chapter Elu Tereifot (Ḥullin 42a). Therefore, since it cannot survive, he has consecrated a thing upon which life depends, and therefore [Rabbi Yehuda] concedes.
rashi:b6.2: And Rava holds a tereifa can survive: And it is not a thing upon which life depends.
tosafot:b6.1: Rav Ḥisda holds in accordance with the one who says a tereifa cannot survive, and Rava holds in accordance with the one who says a tereifa can survive: In the first chapter of Bekhorot (3a) this discussion is reversed, with regard to partnership with a gentile, where Rav Ḥisda holds a tereifa can survive; and this is one of the reversed discussions in the Talmud. And so we find in other places with regard to the dispute between Abaye and Rava about “the hands prove,” in tractate Nedarim (5b) and in tractate Nazir (62a; see there). However, this requires examination according to what Rava says here, that a tereifa can survive, for in the chapter HaḤoletz (Yevamot 36a) Rava says with regard to an animal that is possibly a tereifa that we wait with it twelve months.
rashi:b7.1: If the thigh and its recess were removed, it is a carcass: Even though it is still alive, it imparts impurity like a carcass, for it is like a dead animal and not like a living one.
rashi:b7.2: Rava holds in accordance with Rabbi Elazar: Therefore, if he consecrated the thigh and its recess, it is a thing upon which life depends.
rashi:b7.3: And Rav Sheshet does not hold in accordance with Rabbi Elazar: In the first chapter of Ḥullin (21a) it explains what “its recess” is: whatever, when [the animal] lies down, appears to be lacking.
gershom:b6.1: Rav Sheshet does not hold in accordance with Rabbi Elazar: That is why he says “with regard to a thing [without which] it dies” immediately, and not that it would still be convulsing. [Evidently they disagree about both.]
gershom:b7.1: And a refutation of all of them: Of Rav Ḥisda, Rabba and Rav Sheshet. [Rabbeinu Gershom writes Rabba where the daf has Rava.]
rashi:b10.1: This is what it is saying: The statement of Rabbi Yosei appears correct to Rabbi Yehuda: For Rabbi Yehuda concedes to him with regard to a thing upon which life depends.
gershom:b8.1: Rather, [the baraita] is incomplete and this is what it is teaching, etc. And [the amora’im] are not difficult.
rashi:b11.1: With regard to a bird, what is the halakha: He asks according to Rabbi Yosei: If one consecrated the leg of a bird, of a turtledove or a young pigeon, does the sanctity spread through all of it or not?
rashi:b11.2: The Merciful One states “animal”: In this verse, “anything of it that one gives,” both “animal” and “offering” are written.
gershom:b9.1: With regard to a bird, what is the halakha: [According to] Rabbi Yosei, if one consecrated a leg of a bird, is all of it sacred as well or not? Do we say: The Merciful One states “offering” (“And if it is an animal of which they bring an offering to the Lord”), and this too is an offering?
rashi:b12.1: If one consecrated a limb for its value, what is the halakha as to inherent sanctity descending upon it: Upon the whole animal, so that it is sacrificed as a burnt offering? Do we say according to Rabbi Yosei: since he consecrated one limb for its value, the sanctity spread to the whole animal for its value; and since sanctity of value descended upon the whole animal, inherent sanctity descends upon it, since its body itself is fit for a burnt offering? Why should he need to sell it and bring a burnt offering with its value? Therefore it is necessarily consecrated with inherent sanctity.
rashi:b12.2: Two [claims of] “since”: One, that he consecrated only a limb, and for its value, and we need to say: since [the sanctity] takes effect on the limb, it takes effect on the whole animal for its value; and [two,] since all of it descends [into sanctity] for its value, all of it also descends into inherent sanctity.
rashi:b13.1: Resolve it from his own statement: That certainly inherent sanctity descends upon it.
rashi:b13.2: For Rava said: If one consecrated a male: A male ram. And Rava specified a male because Rava is speaking of a burnt offering, and a female is not fit for a burnt offering, so one could not speak of inherent sanctity.
rashi:b13.3: For its value: To bring a burnt offering with its value. It is consecrated with inherent sanctity, and he cannot sell it, since it itself is fit for a burnt offering, and it itself shall be sacrificed as a burnt offering. And here too, since according to Rabbi Yosei the sanctity descends upon all of it by means of the limb, it is consecrated inherently as well.
gershom:b10.1: Resolve it from what you said: If one consecrated a male [fit for a burnt offering, consecrating it] for its value, it is consecrated with inherent sanctity.
rashi:b14.1: There, where he consecrated all of it: And there is only one [claim of] “since.”
gershom:b11.1: There: [Because] he consecrated all of it for its value, and since sanctity of [value descends upon all of it], inherent sanctity [also] descends upon [all of it].
gershom:b12.1: Another version: One [claim of] “since” we say [that is what we said]. Two [claims of] “since” [since he consecrated one limb, all of it is consecrated, etc., and since it is consecrated for its value, it is consecrated with inherent sanctity] we do not say.
rashi:b15.1: If one consecrated a limb, what is the halakha with regard to shearing: With regard to labor you need not ask, for it is prohibited, since it weakens [the animal].
rashi:b15.2: Yours and others’: A gentile. If you have a firstborn in partnership with a gentile, it is permitted to shear it. Here too, since non-sacred and consecrated are partners in it, it is permitted.
rashi:b16.1: There: With regard to the firstborn, no sanctity at all descended upon it, even upon the Jew’s share, for partnership with a gentile exempts [an animal] from firstborn status. Here, sanctity descended upon that limb.
rashi:b16.2: It is not in his power to consecrate it: Since the gentile has a partnership in it.
tosafot:b16.1: There, inherent sanctity did not descend upon it: Rashi explained that [the Gemara] holds that partnership with a gentile exempts from firstborn status. But in the first chapter of Bekhorot (3b) it says [this] even according to the one who says partnership with a gentile does not exempt; and what it says there, “sanctity did not descend upon it,” means [sanctity] to be sacrificed.
gershom:b13.1: This too is “yours and others’”: For only one limb of it is consecrated and the rest of the body is non-sacred. He said to him: There, sanctity did not descend upon all of it, since half of it belongs to the gentile, and the gentile’s share is not consecrated. Here, where all of it is his, sanctity descends upon all of it, and all of it is prohibited for shearing. [The note ends with the unclear words “He consecrated a lamb, as in another version.”]
rashi:b17.1: If one consecrated its skin: Of an animal, what is the halakha with regard to labor? With regard to shearing you need not ask, for it does not weaken the skin; but labor weakens the skin.
rashi:b17.2: Due to the weakening of the fetus: And here too there is weakening of the skin.
gershom:b14.1: The skin, what is the halakha with regard to labor: That is, he is not asking about shearing, for it is certainly prohibited because of the weakening of the skin; he is asking about labor. [So the text reads; Rashi writes that shearing does not weaken the skin.]
rashi:b18.1: By rabbinic law: And he is asking about Torah law, [whether] one would receive lashes for it.
gershom:b15.1: Come hear: One who says, “That which is in the womb of this animal is a burnt offering,” it is permitted for shearing and prohibited for labor, due to the weakening of the fetus. Here too, labor weakens the skin and is prohibited, for when [the animal] is fat the skin is better. He said to him: You cannot resolve it from here, for when it teaches here “prohibited for labor,” it teaches that it is by rabbinic law and not by Torah law, and I am asking about the skin, whether it is prohibited by Torah law. If so, if it is by rabbinic law, then let even shearing be prohibited by rabbinic law with regard to the fetus. He said to him, etc.
rashi:b19.1: It is a peace offering and its offspring is non-sacred: He consecrated a pregnant animal except for its fetus, so that according to everyone the fetus is not sacred.
rashi:b19.2: According to the one who said offspring of sacrificial animals are sanctified at their coming into being: That is, a person consecrated an animal and afterward it became pregnant, and I ask according to the one who says offspring of sacrificial animals are sanctified at their coming into being. Now, in any event, the fetus is not consecrated, and he slaughtered the mother inside, in the courtyard: is the offspring a non-sacred animal [slaughtered] in the courtyard, and he is liable, since the fetus was not consecrated, or not?
tosafot:b19.1: It is a peace offering and its offspring is non-sacred, and he slaughtered it inside, what is the halakha: That is, whether the offspring is prohibited as a non-sacred animal [slaughtered] in the courtyard. And it seems that he could have resolved it from that [baraita] above, “one who slaughters the sin offering and finds in it a live four-month-old,” which implies that it is not [prohibited as] a non-sacred animal in the courtyard.
gershom:b16.1: And according to the one who says offspring of sacrificial animals are sanctified at their coming into being: At the time of their birth and not [from] their mother’s womb. [Do we say this offspring is non-sacred] only from the time of their coming into being at birth, or perhaps with regard to non-sacred status it is non-sacred even in its mother’s womb, and he would be liable?
